newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin sees tough U.S. summit, sets conditions.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin sees tough U.S. summit, sets conditions.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin said on Friday next week's Russia-U.S. summit in Helsinki would be the hardest since he became Russian president in 1991 and he stepped up opposition to NATO membership for any former Soviet republics.

Yeltsin said differences over NATO's expansion plans could prove unbridgeable at the summit next Wednesday and Thursday with U.S. President Bill Clinton, but he told Russian media chiefs that would not be a tragedy and he was ready for compromise.
The talks "will be the hardest in all the history of Russian-American relations", Interfax news agency quoted the 66-year-old Kremlin leader as saying.

But he added: "In a recent telephone conversation Clinton made clear the United States is interested in compromise, and so am I. We are for a compromise which would not abuse the security of the Russian Federation."

Yeltsin's comments may lower expectations of a major breakthrough in the row with NATO over its plans to take in members from eastern and central Europe. Moscow says such moves would threaten its security.
But the remarks appeared intended partly for a domestic audience, showing he is not about to sell out Russia's interests at the summit.
Yeltsin wants to avoid relations with the West freezing over NATO's enlargement but cannot be seen by nationalists and communists to capitulate to Moscow's former Cold War foe.

As if to highlight the domestic pressure Yeltsin faces, the communist opposition-dominated lower house of parliament on Friday passed a resolution demanding that the president strongly oppose NATO expansion plans during the Helsinki summit.
The row over NATO's plans is set to dominate the summit, but arms control and economic issues are also on the agenda.
Final preparations will be made by Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov during a trip to Washington at the weekend which could go a long way to determining the outcome of the summit.
Many foreign policy experts in Moscow say a breakthrough is possible in Helsinki towards an agreement charting future relations between NATO and Russia.
But a final deal is not expected until much closer to a NATO summit in July at which the alliance is expected to issue invitations to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
"We and the American side may disagree over questions of NATO expansion at the meeting in Helsinki but it is not worth making a tragedy out of this," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying.
He ruled out any concessions which might threaten Russia's defence capability.

Yeltsin said one "categoric condition" for Russia was that NATO should not try to draw in any of the 12 former Soviet republics which make up the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) or the Baltic states of Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia.

"In connection with this, the Russian leadership is alarmed by contacts between NATO and the leaderships of these countries, including the trip by alliance Secretary-General Javier Solana to a series of CIS states," Yeltsin said.

He was referring to recent, much-criticised visits by Solana to several CIS states. Russia regards some of the former Soviet republics in Central Asia as forming its strategic underbelly and sees the Baltic states as a buffer against the West.

Yeltsin's comments highlighted Moscow's sensitivity over the Baltic states and moves by NATO which would mean the area separating Russia and its western enclave of Kaliningrad became part of the Western alliance.
Russia is also sensitive about the long-term prospect of Ukraine joining NATO. Kiev does not oppose NATO expansion and has not ruled out eventually joining the alliance.
